It presents rewards as tied to recruiting people who invest and says an affiliate link generates payment when others join, although the exact destination, contract terms, payouts, losses, and independent verification are not established.

opening.argument: The speaker presents personal goals and rough, openly uncertain estimates, not a guaranteed investment outcome. He calls the $250,000 target “an audacious goal” and describes it as his own one-year objective, which is materially different from promising viewers they will achieve it. His valuation language is also tentative rather than authoritative: he repeatedly revises what 0.4 Ethereum might be worth. The video therefore supports an aspirational personal account with uncertainty, not a definite promise of returns.

citations.quote: I know this as an audacious goal, right?
my goal is to make $250,000 just on this one account
0.4 I believe right now was about $78. Actually wait 0.4 is maybe a little bit more than that

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats discussion of joining and affiliate compensation as proof of a scam, but those statements establish only that the speaker describes a participation process and his own referral arrangement. They do not establish that he guaranteed viewers profits, concealed risk, or represented his personal goal as a promised result. The uncertain valuation and explicit characterization of the target as audacious support a non-guaranteed presentation.

citations.quote: I know this as an audacious goal, right?
this is my affiliate link right if you guys see this is an affiliate link so I get paid when somebody joins my team

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling a target “audacious” does not turn the video into a warning or remove its solicitation. The speaker still directs viewers toward joining and earning, while describing an affiliate link that pays him when someone joins. Uncertainty about the value of Ethereum concerns arithmetic, not whether recruitment-based compensation is being promoted.

opening.argument: The video's dominant format is a screen-recorded walkthrough showing how the speaker's websites, accounts, goals, wallet setup, and funnel operate. He explicitly explains that he is giving viewers simple steps and demonstrates editing and transferring a funnel into a new account. That is an operational tutorial and personal demonstration: viewers are shown processes and tools, rather than being given independently verified claims about an investment's safety or guaranteed performance. The presence of a call to action does not erase the instructional format.

you can see, I have this exact same website that I was just using a few seconds ago

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution cites instructions to join, but instruction is exactly what the video visibly and verbally performs: setting up a wallet, navigating pages, and configuring a funnel. The excerpts do not establish that the demonstration is fabricated, that the tools are nonexistent, or that every viewer is promised income. A practical walkthrough can include a referral link without becoming a scam claim.

citations.quote: what I've done is, I made simple one, 2, 3 steps

I instantly ported that into my account

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial framing is not neutral: the walkthrough is designed to move viewers through registration, wallet purchase, and joining the contract. The speaker calls the funnel a team-building tool and supplies it to people who join. Demonstrating the mechanics therefore supports promotion of the recruitment process rather than merely explaining technology.

opening.argument: The evidence is also consistent with ordinary promotion of digital services and referral tools: the speaker describes a website builder, paid traffic, email capture, domains, and an affiliate program. Those are recognizable marketing services, not proof of a fraudulent product. The record does not establish a guaranteed return, a promised recovery of funds, or any credential request. It also does not establish what the reported amounts represent, so the claim that they are scam proceeds would require an inference beyond the supplied material.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution identifies recruitment and payment language, but referral compensation is also common in ordinary marketing services. Its excerpts do not show that the speaker guarantees a return, misstates a contract, or takes credentials. Even the reported $700 is not characterized in the supplied record as profit, withdrawals, or a promised outcome, so it cannot alone establish a scam mechanism.

citations.quote: aspire builder also has an affiliate program right you guys see that you get 20 anytime somebody joins aspire builder

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The ordinary-service comparison omits the central condition the speaker actually describes: another person joins his team and invests before he earns. The video also tells viewers to purchase Ethereum and join the contract, then identifies an affiliate link that pays when someone joins. Those are recruitment-linked financial participation steps, not merely promotion of a website builder.
